situation.note: I want to stop my anxiety medicines and use only meditation and Gita. my doctor says no. what does Krishna say, should I trust my faith over medicine?

understanding.bridge: The doctor and the Gita are both asking you to hold your ground. What they disagree on is whether the ground is faith or medicine.
understanding.week_thesis: The week moves from being torn between faith and medicine to a steadiness that holds both without choosing between them.

week_beats.hook: You recognise the restlessness and the tornness between faith and medicine, named without judgement.
week_beats.diagnose: You see that the unacted-on decision between two authorities is what feeds the restlessness.
week_beats.steady: You hold that your duty is to be well, and the means that steadies the mind are not its enemy.
week_beats.act: You try speaking to your doctor and doing one meditation, letting both be part of the path.
week_beats.story: A seeker torn between two paths to wisdom shows you that the path is not the enemy, only the refusal to walk it.

understanding.core_struggle: Wants to stop anxiety medicine and use only meditation and the Gita, but is torn between faith and the doctor's warning.
understanding.mirror: You want to lay down the pills and trust the Gita instead, and your doctor is saying no.
understanding.insight: Your faith and your doctor both want you to be well. The question is whether they can both be right, and what it means to trust one without abandoning the other.

queries.hook: The mind will not settle, and the question of whether to trust faith over medicine is making it worse.
queries.diagnose: Doubt and delay feed each other; waiting to feel ready keeps you stuck between two authorities, and the unacted-on decision weighs more than the work.
queries.steady: Your duty is to be well; the means that steadies the mind are not the enemy of the mind that seeks steadiness.
queries.act: Speak to your doctor about what you are feeling, and practise the one meditation you can do today while you both decide.
queries.story: A seeker who was torn between two paths to wisdom, who learned that the path is not the enemy, but the refusal to walk it is.

verse.speaker: Arjuna
verse.setting: Arjuna confesses the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; Krishna answers.
verse.sanskrit: चञ्चलं हि मनः कृष्ण प्रमाथि बलवद्दृढम् । तस्याहं निग्रहं मन्ये वायोरिव सुदुष्करम् ॥
verse.line: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.
verse.translation: For the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. I think it is as hard to hold as the wind.
verse.why: The mind is hard to hold, but practice and letting go train it.

prasang.title: Mastering the mind
prasang.summary: Arjuna says the mind is restless, stormy and stubborn. Krishna agrees, and says practice and letting go can train it.
prasang.lesson: The mind is hard to hold, but practice and letting go train it.

verse.meaning: Arjuna stands on the battlefield, his body weak, his mind racing. He tells Krishna that his thoughts are wild and hard to control, like trying to catch the wind. Krishna agrees. The mind is strong and stubborn, but it can be trained. It does not happen all at once. It happens through practice, and through letting go of the need to force it.
verse.for_you: You sit with your phone and your mind races. Your doctor wants you to keep taking your medicine. The Gita wants you to trust your practice. Both are asking you to hold your ground, but they disagree on what the ground is. The restlessness is real.
verse.try_today: Notice one moment when your mind races without trying to fix it.
verse.scene_line: You are standing in the middle of the battlefield, unsure which path to take.
asks: How do I practice without forcing my mind to stop?
Is the restlessness a sign that I am doing something wrong?

verse.speaker: Yama
verse.setting: Nachiketa has refused wealth and long life; Yama begins teaching.
verse.sanskrit: श्रेयश्च प्रेयश्च मनुष्यमेतस्तौ सम्परीत्य विविनक्ति धीरः । श्रेयो हि धीरोऽभि प्रेयसो वृणीते प्रेयो मन्दो योगक्षेमाद्वृणीते ॥
verse.line: The good and the pleasant both knock. The wise choose the good; the foolish grab the pleasant.
verse.translation: The good and the pleasant both come to a person. The wise one examines them and tells them apart. The wise chooses the good over the pleasant; the dull chooses the pleasant, for getting and keeping.
verse.why: Every day offers a choice between what feels good and what is good.

prasang.title: The good and the pleasant
prasang.summary: Yama praises Nachiketa for choosing the good over the pleasant. He explains that both come to every person, and the wise tell them apart, while the foolish choose what is pleasant and lose their way.
prasang.lesson: Every day offers a choice between what feels good and what is good.

verse.meaning: Nachiketa, the boy who asked for the secret of what comes after death, has just turned away from every worldly reward. Yama, the lord of death, begins his teaching. He says that every person meets two forces. One is the pleasant, which promises immediate comfort. The other is the good, which asks for patience and leads to lasting well-being. The wise person looks at both and chooses the good. The dull person grabs the pleasant, hoping to keep it forever. The choice is not about being harsh or soft.
verse.for_you: Your doctor and your Gita both want you to be well, but they are asking you to let go of something different. The medicine asks you to let go of the fear of side effects. The Gita asks you to let go of the need to control the outcome.
verse.try_today: Notice the moment you feel pulled toward one authority over the other.
verse.scene_line: You are the one who must choose between the pleasant and the good.
asks: How do I let both the doctor and the Gita stand at the same time?
What is the pleasant I am trying to grab in this choice?

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna answers Arjuna's question: what does a person of steady mind look like?
verse.sanskrit: श्री भगवानुवाचप्रजहाति यदा कामान् सर्वान् पार्थ मनोगतान् । आत्मन्येवात्मना तुष्टः स्थितप्रज्ञस्तदोच्यते ॥
verse.line: When you stop chasing every desire and find contentment within yourself, your wisdom becomes steady.
verse.translation: The Blessed Lord said: When a person gives up all the desires of the mind and is content in the self by the self, then he is called one of steady wisdom.
verse.why: Steadiness is built by guarding attention; anger starts with what you dwell on.

prasang.title: The person of steady wisdom
prasang.summary: Arjuna asks how a steady person speaks, sits and walks. Krishna describes someone content within, unshaken by sorrow, master of the senses, and traces how dwelling on things leads to anger and ruin.
prasang.lesson: Steadiness is built by guarding attention; anger starts with what you dwell on.

verse.meaning: Arjuna asks what a steady person looks like. Krishna answers by describing someone who is not shaken by sorrow or desire, whose mind is calm and whose senses are under control. This steadiness comes not from forcing the mind to be still, but from giving up the chase for things outside of it. When you stop running after what you do not have, and find a quiet place inside yourself, your wisdom becomes solid. The mind does not need to be fought. It needs to be let go of.
verse.for_you: Your mind is restless right now because it is caught between two different calls. Your doctor asks you to keep taking your medicine. The Gita asks you to find contentment within. Both are asking you to be well. You do not have to choose between them.
verse.try_today: Notice when your mind starts to chase the idea of stopping the medicine, and gently let that thought go.
verse.scene_line: You stand in your own mind, offered two paths and asked to choose one.
asks: How do I stop chasing one path and find quiet inside?
Can I be content while the medicine is still in my body?

verse.speaker: Ribhu
verse.setting: Ribhu on inner stillness in an active life.
verse.sanskrit: बहिःकृत्रिमसंरंभो हृदि संरम्भवर्जितः । कर्ता बहिरकर्तान्तर्लोके विहर शुद्धधीः ॥
verse.line: Be busy on the outside and unhurried inside. Act fully, but don't let it agitate you.
verse.translation: Outwardly busy, inwardly free of agitation; a doer on the outside, a non-doer within: move through the world with a clear mind.
verse.why: Live fully in the world while staying unhurried inside.

prasang.title: How a free person lives
prasang.summary: Ribhu describes how a free person lives among others: letting go of what is lost, taking up what comes, doing the work at hand, speaking gently, busy outside and calm inside, and treating the whole world as family.
prasang.lesson: Live fully in the world while staying unhurried inside.

verse.meaning: Ribhu is teaching Nidagha how a free person lives in the world. He says that you can be active on the outside and unhurried on the inside. You do the work at hand, you let go of what is lost, and you take up what comes. You move through the world with a clear mind, acting fully but not letting the doing agitate you. The point is that you do not have to choose between being busy and being still.
verse.for_you: Your mind is restless. The ground is not faith or medicine. It is the duty to be well. You can be busy on the outside and unhurried inside.
verse.try_today: Notice when your work agitates you, and let your inside stay unhurried.
verse.scene_line: You are busy on the outside and unhurried inside, moving through the world with a clear mind.
asks: How do I hold my duty to be well without choosing between faith and medicine?
How do I let the doing of my day settle my mind instead of agitating it?

verse.speaker: Vasishtha
verse.setting: The sage Vasishtha to Bharat, shattered by his father's death and Ram's exile.
verse.sanskrit: तात हृदयँ धीरजु धरहु करहु जो अवसर आजु। उठे भरत गुर बचन सुनि करन कहेउ सबु साजु ॥
verse.line: Keep courage in your heart, and do what today asks of you.
verse.translation: "Child, keep courage in your heart, and do what this moment asks of you today." Hearing his teacher, Bharat rose and had everything made ready.
verse.why: When head and heart disagree, go and face the person you think you wronged.

prasang.title: Bharat refuses the throne
prasang.summary: After the funeral, Vasishtha, the ministers and Kausalya all urge Bharat to rule, as his father wished. Bharat says the advice is right and his heart still isn't at peace; the crown means nothing without Ram. He decides to go to the forest, admit his fault, and trust his brother to forgive.
prasang.story_hook: Everyone agreed the throne was his, and Bharat could not bring himself to sit on it.
prasang.lesson: When head and heart disagree, go and face the person you think you wronged.

verse.meaning: Vasishtha speaks to Bharat, who is shattered by his father's death and Ram's exile. The ministers urge Bharat to take the throne, but Bharat feels the crown is worthless without Ram. Vasishtha tells him to keep courage in his heart and do what this moment asks. Bharat then rises and prepares to go to the forest, admitting his fault to Ram.
verse.for_you: You are torn between the doctor's warning and your own faith. The verse asks you to face the person you feel you wronged. Your doctor is not your enemy, and your faith is not your escape. Go and speak to your doctor. Do one meditation.

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Arjuna asks which devotee is best; Krishna offers a ladder of practices.
verse.line: Practice is good, understanding better, meditation better still. But letting go of results brings peace at once.
verse.translation: Knowledge is better than mere practice; meditation is better than knowledge; giving up the fruit of action is better than meditation. From that renunciation, peace follows immediately.
verse.why: If the ideal is too hard, take the next step down, and keep going.
verse.misuse: Not 'stop caring how things turn out'. Peace comes from releasing the grip, not from indifference.

prasang.title: Form or formless: which devotee is best, and the ways to reach him
prasang.summary: Krishna says devotion to a personal form is easier, then offers a ladder: fix your mind; if not, practise; if not, work for me; if not, let go of results. Letting go brings peace at once.
prasang.lesson: If the ideal is too hard, take the next step down, and keep going.

verse.meaning: Arjuna asks which devotee is best. Krishna offers a ladder of practices. He says knowledge is better than practice, meditation better than knowledge. But letting go of results brings peace at once. If the ideal is too hard, take the next step down, and keep going. Peace comes from releasing the grip, not from indifference.
verse.for_you: The question is whether you can let go of the result of choosing one over the other. Your mind is restless because it is trying to win a war it does not need to fight.
verse.try_today: Let go of the result of choosing one over the other.
verse.scene_line: You are at the bottom of the ladder, trying to climb with both feet on the same rung.
asks: How do I let go of the result of choosing one over the other?

story.title: Learned seers find no peace and go to Ganesha
story.story_hook: They knew every verse of every Veda, and still could not sleep.
story.summary: Seers who had received all the Vedas still found no peace, so they went to Ganesha's world and took refuge in him. Ganesha tells them that though he has no form, loving devotees see him in the form they long for, and that knowing his highest form brings lasting peace.
story.lesson: Learning alone may not settle the heart; turning to God can.

anchor.line: Lord, no peace came to our minds. So we have come to you for refuge.
anchor.translation: So no peace came into our minds, Lord. We have come to your world and taken refuge in you.

story.for_you: You have read every line of your texts, yet your mind still races. The doctor and the Gita are not two enemies. They are two paths up the same mountain. The refusal to walk is what keeps you restless. Trust the path, and let your feet move.
